questions.q: Why does this lesson say every integration deserves the same deliberate security design as a human user's access, and arguably more?
options: Because integrations are always more secure than human users by default

Because an integration crosses the org boundary on a recurring, automated basis, its credentials often don't expire the way a human session does, and a compromised credential can act at machine speed and volume
Because Salesforce does not allow integrations to be audited
Because integrations never require any OAuth scopes
questions.explain: An integration is a deliberate, recurring crossing of the org boundary, and unlike a human session, its credentials may not expire on a predictable schedule -- a compromise can be exploited at machine speed and volume, which is why it deserves at least as much design attention as human access.

questions.q: What do OAuth scopes configured on a Connected App actually control?
options: The field-level security settings for every user in the org
The physical network location integrations are allowed to connect from
The maximum set of permissions any client authenticating through that Connected App is allowed to request -- a client can ask for a subset, never more
The number of API calls an org can make per day
questions.explain: Connected App OAuth scopes cap what any authenticating client can ever request; a client's actual scope request must be a subset of what the Connected App permits -- never broader.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that scoping a Connected App narrowly (e.g., requesting only `api` instead of `full`) doesn't fully solve least privilege on its own?
options: Because OAuth scopes have no actual security effect
Because `full` scope is always required for any integration to function
Because Connected Apps cannot be scoped at all in current Salesforce releases

Because the integration user it authenticates as still goes through every boundary from Lesson 1 (CRUD, sharing, field-level security) -- an over-permissioned integration user profile undoes most of the scope's benefit
questions.explain: The Connected App scope controls what the client can ask for; the integration user's own profile and permission sets still govern what it can actually touch once authenticated -- both layers need to be scoped correctly, not just one.

questions.q: In the Named Credential model, what is the structural relationship between an External Credential and a Named Credential?
options: An External Credential holds the actual authentication details; a Named Credential references that External Credential plus the callout endpoint URL, so Apex/Flow can call out without hardcoding secrets
They are the same object with two different names
A Named Credential holds authentication details; an External Credential only stores the endpoint URL
External Credentials are only used for inbound integrations, never outbound callouts
questions.explain: The External Credential holds the authentication details (OAuth settings, parameters); the Named Credential references it along with the callout endpoint, letting business logic make callouts without the secret or URL being hardcoded into Apex or Flow.

questions.q: A logistics partner's nightly batch job needs to pull Shipment records with no individual human session involved, while a separate feature needs each warehouse employee's actions on the partner's portal to be individually attributable. Which authentication model fits each case?
options: Per-User for the batch job, Named Principal for the employee lookup feature
Named Principal for the batch job (one shared service identity, no individual session to attribute), and Per-User for the employee lookup feature (individual accountability needed)
Named Principal for both, since it is always the simpler and preferred choice
Per-User for both, since Named Principal cannot be used for scheduled jobs
questions.explain: Named Principal fits backend, service-account-style automation like a scheduled batch job with no human session to attribute. Per-User fits cases where the external system needs to know specifically which individual is acting, which matters for the employee lookup feature's accountability needs.
